questions.prompt: After the two edits, what changes in each draft? Explain what let fixes, what copying a struct separates, and what sharing a class object keeps together.
questions.scenario: In this made-up example, Selection is a struct with var specialtyID: Int64? and let notes: Notes. Notes is a class whose text can change. original uses let. edited uses var and starts as a copy of original. Run edited.specialtyID = 20 and edited.notes.text = "Changed".
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin val and Swift let both constrain reassignment, but a Kotlin mutable data-class assignment aliases an object while Swift struct assignment gives value semantics. Kotlin data-class copy is also shallow for nested references; neither copy recursively clones mutable objects.
rubric: Predicts separate specialtyID values and the same changed notes.text in both drafts.
Explains why assigning original.specialtyID through let is rejected.
Distinguishes equal contents from the same class object, tested with ===.
Explains that arrays behave as separate values without promising that storage copies immediately.
questions.answerHTML:
The two drafts have separate specialty fields but point to one Notes object. Changing edited.specialtyID leaves the original identifier alone. Changing the shared object's text makes both drafts read Changed. A binding is the name used to reach a value. let prevents changing the struct through that name, including assigning original.specialtyID. It does not freeze an object reached through a field.

Use === to check whether references reach the same class object. == checks equal values when the type supplies equality, usually through Equatable conformance. Swift arrays also have observable value semantics, although their storage may be shared until mutation requires separation. That implementation does not imply recursive cloning of elements that are classes. For an independently editable draft, use value fields throughout the mutable domain or explicitly copy the referenced data. State the required independence before choosing the representation.
followUps: Which edits remain possible if edited also uses let?
If you copy an array of Notes objects, which changes stay separate and which are shared?
pitfalls: Saying a struct copy also copies every object it points to.
Saying let freezes all objects reachable through a value.

questions.prompt: Handle a missing procedure ID safely. Keep missing names, empty names, and display defaults separate instead of storing made-up replacement values.
questions.scenario: A made-up form has procedureID: Int64? and patientName: String?. It displays patientName ?? "Unknown" but submits procedureID with a force unwrap. A teammate wants to store -1 for a missing ID and turn an empty name into nil.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin nullable values and Swift optionals both represent absence. Kotlin's Elvis operator resembles ??, but neither operator validates a present empty string; Swift guard let introduces a nonoptional binding whose failure branch must leave the scope.
rubric: Distinguishes a missing name, a present empty name, and a label used only for display.
Uses guard let and deliberately returns or reports an error when the procedure is missing.
Keeps display defaults out of the stored model.
Explains that optional chaining skips missing values but does not check present contents.
questions.answerHTML:
nil means no name was supplied. An empty string means a name value was supplied but contains no characters. patientName ?? "Unknown" replaces only nil, so an empty name still displays as empty. Decide separately whether blank input is valid. Keep missing IDs as nil; storing -1 risks letting later code treat a made-up ID as a real selection.

At submission, use guard let procedure = draft.procedureID else { return }, with the failure branch presenting the agreed selection requirement or returning a typed failure. After the guard, procedure is nonoptional. A force unwrap instead traps if the assumption is violated. Test missing and present identifiers, plus nil, empty, and nonempty names. Optional chaining skips access when its receiver is absent; it still permits invalid present content. Display defaults should explain a state without silently changing the submitted data.
followUps: If whitespace-only names are rejected, where would you apply that rule?
When should a function return an optional, and when should it throw a validation error?
pitfalls: Expecting ?? to replace an empty string.
Force-unwrapping because the current test data always has an ID.

questions.prompt: Why should each search result carry its own data, while each cancellation reason has one fixed service code? Show how switch reads the result data and handles every case.
questions.scenario: SearchState has idle, loading, loaded(providers: [String]), and failed(message: String). CancellationReason is a separate enum with fixed String codes sent to a service. Use these made-up types to explain associated values and raw values.
questions.androidBridge: A Kotlin sealed hierarchy with payload-bearing subtypes resembles a Swift associated-value enum. Kotlin when smart-casts a subtype; Swift switch binds case payloads directly. Raw-value enums represent fixed case identifiers rather than per-instance sealed-state data.
rubric: Distinguishes data for one enum value from a fixed code for a case.
Uses case let .loaded(names) to read the provider array.
Explains why handling every local case without default reveals missing decisions after adding a case.
Handles an unknown service string when raw-value conversion returns nil.
questions.answerHTML:
An associated value is data stored with this particular enum value. One .loaded can carry Ada; another can carry Ben. Each .failed can carry its own message. A raw value is a fixed code for a declared case: the same cancellation reason always has the same service string. A fixed code cannot replace the changing list or message that a search result needs.

Render with an exhaustive switch. The branch case let .loaded(names) extracts the array into a local immutable binding; it does not cast a subclass. Handle its empty array as successful no matches, and give idle, loading, and failure their own behavior. Adding a case then exposes missing decisions at the switches that need updating. Converting an unrecognized service string with a raw-value initializer yields nil; the boundary must choose a deliberate fallback or rejection. The enum describes possible states, while transition rules still require implementation and tests.
followUps: When would checking one case with if case be enough?
What useful extra state, if any, would an optional SearchState add?
pitfalls: Calling every enum's changing data its rawValue.
Using default to hide a new state that needs its own behavior.

questions.prompt: Replace the conflicting search flags with named states. Decide whether offline needs its own case or a failure reason, and explain what happens to old results.
questions.scenario: A made-up screen can say isLoading = true and hasError = true while providers = []. It must distinguish not searched, searching, successful no matches, and a failure the user can retry. Offline behavior may keep old results visible.
questions.androidBridge: Android sealed UI state can replace unrelated LiveData or StateFlow flags, just as Swift enum cases constrain combinations. Neither StateFlow nor an enum enforces legal transitions, cancellation, or retention of prior content by itself.
rubric: Models not searched, searching, successful no matches, and failure separately.
Chooses the offline representation from the user action and rule for retaining content.
Names the conflicting flag combinations the new type prevents.
Tests state changes; does not claim a complete switch proves the workflow correct.
questions.answerHTML:
Represent the screen with one enum value: idle, loading, loaded(providers:), or failed. It can then hold only one of these choices at a time. An empty loaded array means the search finished successfully and found nothing. That calls for changing the search, while a failure may call for retry. Separate flags allowed those different situations to contradict each other.

Add an offline case when it owns meaningfully different behavior, such as a connection explanation and retained previous results. Otherwise a typed reason inside failed can express the distinction without duplicating presentation. If prior content is retained, make that payload and its freshness explicit rather than leaving a hidden array beside the state. Specify start, completion, retry, and replacement transitions and test their visible outcomes. Exhaustive switching forces rendering decisions but cannot decide whether a transition is legal or whether the displayed data belongs to the current request.
followUps: How would loading carry old results that should remain visible?
What test would show that idle and loaded([]) need different behavior?
pitfalls: Treating successful no matches as a failure to retry.
Expecting the compiler to decide which state changes are allowed.

questions.prompt: What does badge() return through FeaturedBadge and through any BadgeNaming? If both callers need the featured behavior, how should the protocol change?
questions.scenario: BadgeNaming declares no required methods. Its extension adds badge(), returning "default". FeaturedBadge adopts BadgeNaming and adds badge(), returning "featured". Call the method first on FeaturedBadge, then on any BadgeNaming containing that same value.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin extension functions are statically selected and provide a useful analogy for Swift extension-only helpers. A Swift protocol requirement with a default implementation participates in protocol dispatch; a Kotlin extension cannot retroactively add interface conformance.
rubric: Predicts featured for the concrete call and default for the protocol-valued call.
Distinguishes an extension helper from a method the protocol requires.
Adds badge() to the protocol when callers need each type's own implementation.
Explains that any hides the concrete type and can contain a struct as well as a class.
questions.answerHTML:
The concrete FeaturedBadge call returns featured. The any BadgeNaming call returns default. Here any means the caller uses a value through its protocol without knowing the concrete type. The protocol never promised a badge method. Its extension only supplied a helper, so the same-named method on FeaturedBadge does not replace that helper for calls through this protocol.

If callers require specialized behavior through the protocol, declare func badge() -> String inside BadgeNaming. The extension can still provide the default implementation, and the conformer supplies its own implementation for the requirement. An existential is a value used through a protocol with its concrete type hidden. Structs as well as classes can meet that protocol. Test the same behavior through the boundary consumers actually use. Testing only the concrete type can miss this discrepancy. Extensions can add methods and computed properties, but cannot introduce stored instance properties to keep hidden badge state.
followUps: When would a helper only in the extension be the intended design?
Why could a fake pass a concrete-type test but fail when used through the protocol?
pitfalls: Calling a same-named extension helper an override.
Assuming any Protocol makes its contained value a reference type.

questions.prompt: Why does try? remove the information needed for retry? What else must change when the function saves its success callback to use after returning?
questions.scenario: A made-up synchronous appointment function evaluates (try? service.appointments()) ?? [] and calls onSuccess. A later version stores onSuccess in a handler so it can call it after the function has returned.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin runCatching followed by getOrDefault(emptyList()) can erase failures like Swift try? followed by ?? []. Kotlin callbacks have no direct @escaping counterpart: Swift uses the annotation to permit a plain closure parameter to outlive its call, without specifying a thread or dispatcher.
rubric: Identifies offline failure and successful empty data as the two merged outcomes.
Preserves errors through propagation or explicit do/catch and distinct callbacks.
Marks a plain callback parameter @escaping when it is stored.
Explains that escaping permits a longer lifetime but promises no thread, capture policy, or eventual call.
questions.answerHTML:
try? turns a thrown error into nil. The following ?? [] turns that nil into an empty list. Now an offline failure and a successful empty response both call onSuccess with no appointments. The caller cannot choose retry correctly. Keep separate success and failure paths with do/catch, or pass the error to the caller that owns the decision.

The original synchronous callbacks need no escaping annotation because they run before the consumer returns. Once the plain callback parameter is stored, mark that parameter @escaping and review the retaining handler and captured objects. Escaping permits a longer lifetime; it establishes neither background execution nor weak capture. Define how often completion can occur and when the handler releases the callback. Test nonempty success, empty success, and offline independently, including cleanup when delayed work is abandoned.
followUps: When would discarding an error with try? match the intended behavior?
Which objects would keep each other alive if the saved callback captured its handler?
pitfalls: Using empty success as the replacement for every failure.
Treating @escaping as a promise of background work or safe object lifetime.

questions.prompt: Draw which object keeps the stored callback alive and which object the callback keeps alive. Why can't deinit clear this loop?
questions.scenario: A made-up Screen stores tapCallback, and that closure reads self.name. Set the outside screen variable to nil. A weak probe still sees the screen. Another variable also holds a saved copy of tapCallback.
questions.androidBridge: JVM tracing garbage collection can reclaim an unreachable object cycle. Swift ARC releases objects when strong ownership ends, so an unreachable strong cycle can persist. A Java WeakReference analogy does not reproduce Swift weak references' automatically nil optional access.
rubric: Draws strong links from Screen to closure and back to Screen.
Explains why clearing the outside variable leaves the loop intact.
Explains why deinit cannot run while the cycle keeps the screen alive.
Uses weak capture so a saved callback can survive and safely skip a missing screen.
questions.answerHTML:
The screen keeps its closure alive, and the closure keeps the screen alive. These strong references form a loop called a retain cycle. Clearing the outside variable removes just one link; the loop remains. ARC, Automatic Reference Counting, releases a class object when its strong owners are gone. deinit runs during that release, so cleanup there cannot break a cycle that prevents release from starting.

For a callback that should tolerate the screen disappearing, use [weak self] and an absent-owner branch such as guard let self else { return }. A saved callback then owns the closure without owning the screen through that capture. Optional invocation skips a missing callback. The guard skips a present callback whose screen has gone. The unwrapped local self temporarily provides strong ownership during its use. Verify the controlled graph with a weak probe after removing known strong owners. Deallocation observations support this experiment without promising exact source-line timing under every optimization setting.
followUps: When should a callback keep its owner alive to finish required work?
Why could unowned trap if the saved callback runs after the screen is released?
pitfalls: Expecting ARC to find and collect unreachable cycles like the JVM collector.
Putting the only way to break the cycle inside deinit.

questions.prompt: After guard let self, what does the inner closure keep alive? Choose who owns queued work that may run after the screen is dismissed.
questions.scenario: Screen owns a queue of callbacks. An outer callback uses [weak self], then guard let self. It stores an inner closure on the screen's queue, and that inner closure uses self. The queue may keep the work forever.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin coroutine or callback captures can also retain a screen beyond its intended lifecycle. Lifecycle cancellation is a separate policy in both systems; Swift's outer weak capture does not automatically apply to a nested closure, and ARC cycles differ from JVM reachability collection.
rubric: Identifies the inner closure's capture of unwrapped self as strong.
Draws the possible Screen → queue → closure → Screen cycle.
Distinguishes retention with a proven release path from work kept indefinitely.
Chooses weak screen updates or a separate operation owner according to what must finish.
questions.answerHTML:
A weak reference reaches an object without keeping it alive. But guard let self creates a strong local reference for the outer callback's body. An inner stored closure can capture that reference strongly. Draw screen → queue → inner closure → screen: a new retain cycle is possible. Writing weak on the outer closure does not make the inner closure's reference weak.

Decide whether the queued operation belongs to the screen. If its only purpose is updating a visible screen, give the inner callback its own weak capture and define removal or cancellation when the flow ends. If a save must finish after dismissal, a dedicated operation owner can retain the service and data it needs, while treating screen updates separately. Strong retention until a reliable completion and release path is bounded ownership; work queued indefinitely lacks that assurance. Inspect completion, cancellation, and queue clearing, then use a controlled pending callback to test release. Replacing weak with unowned would substitute a lifetime assumption and possible trap for an ownership policy.
followUps: What evidence would show when the queued work releases its owner?
How would capturing a copied String instead of self change the links?
pitfalls: Assuming nested closures inherit an outer weak capture.
Choosing unowned merely because work usually finishes quickly.

questions.prompt: Which setting controls source-language checking, and which controls whether an API works on the oldest supported iOS? Explain the build choices separately.
questions.scenario: A made-up package declares tools 5.9 and minimum iOS 17. A newer compiler builds it. A neighboring target explicitly uses Swift 6 language mode. Decide what you must inspect for the package's own target.
questions.androidBridge: A Gradle module resembles a build target, and build types or flavors help reason about configurations. An Xcode scheme plans actions across targets rather than defining a flavor; Swift tools version, language mode, SDK, and deployment target are separate axes just as Gradle, Kotlin compiler, and Android SDK settings are distinct.
rubric: Separates compiler, package tools version, language mode, SDK, and deployment target.
Defines target, scheme, configuration, and destination as different build choices.
Finds this target's mode instead of inferring it from a neighbor.
Explains why an API in the SDK may still be unavailable on the minimum runtime.
questions.answerHTML:
The compiler is the program that checks and translates the source. The package's tools version declares the minimum tooling and manifest features; it also influences defaults. Language mode selects the language rules used for a target. These are separate settings. A newer compiler does not put every target into Swift 6 mode. Check this target's effective settings rather than copying the answer from its neighbor.

The SDK supplies compile-time platform APIs, while the deployment target states the oldest supported runtime. An API present in the SDK may still need availability handling for that runtime. A target defines a component, its sources, dependencies, and output. A configuration supplies build settings; a scheme plans actions using targets; a destination selects where an action runs. Record all of these when diagnosing a build. A SwiftPM product exposes targets to consumers, and its product or package name need not equal the imported module name.
followUps: Where would you find evidence of this target's effective language mode?
Why can a package expose several products without giving the whole package one import name?
pitfalls: Assuming a newer compiler means every target uses Swift 6 language rules.
Treating minimum supported iOS as the SDK or package tools version.

questions.prompt: Choose the next useful check for a missing module, a UIKit import in a host test, and tests that compile but never run. What does each check actually prove?
questions.scenario: FoundationLab is a made-up package tested on the development computer. A learner adds a UIKit-dependent test, sees a missing-module error elsewhere, and gets no executed tests from a generated workspace. They suggest regenerating everything and disabling signing.
questions.androidBridge: Gradle dependency graphs, source sets, test tasks, and test runners provide useful diagnostic categories. SwiftPM host tests and Xcode destination-based tests have different platform contracts; an Xcode scheme's test action is not an Android variant, and generic signing changes do not resolve module discovery.
rubric: Checks the dependency and exported product for the module the target actually imports.
Checks platform and destination for the UIKit test.
Checks test source inclusion, test-framework discovery, and the scheme's test action.
States the limits of standalone compilation, swift test, and an app-hosted run.
questions.answerHTML:
Find the first useful error and ask which boundary failed. For a missing module, check the consuming target's dependency, exported product, actual import name, source membership, and platform support. A module is the code unit named by an import. UIKit tests need an iOS target and destination; a host-only test route is not enough. Keep pure model tests independent of UIKit where possible.

Compilation without executed tests requires checking the test target's source glob, framework discovery conventions, and the selected scheme's test action. Listing a workspace verifies structure, not that it builds or runs. Keep the pure model lab on swift test for fast behavioral feedback and use Xcode for platform integration. Record the selected toolchain, target, configuration, and destination with results. Regenerating or changing signing without a related diagnostic can obscure the cause. A passing package test validates that package's behavior, not navigation, signing, or a full application.
followUps: How would you diagnose importing a product name that differs from its module name?
What test-result artifact would prove a discovered test ran?
pitfalls: Calling every failure an Xcode issue without locating the failing boundary.
Reporting passing host tests as proof that the iOS app integration works.

questions.prompt: Describe a small search-loading function and tests for its rules. How would you prove that missing specialty stops the function before it calls the service?
questions.scenario: SearchDraft has optional specialty and procedure IDs and a query. Missing specialty blocks search; missing procedure is allowed. The injected synchronous service can return names, return [], or throw an offline error.
questions.androidBridge: A Kotlin interface and deterministic fake are analogous to a Swift protocol and fake. Swift struct drafts have value semantics unlike assignment of mutable Kotlin data-class objects; Swift Testing @Test and #expect are not JUnit annotations or assertions despite similar behavioral roles.
rubric: Checks specialty before calling the injected service.
Keeps successful [] separate from offline failure.
Uses a recording fake or spy to prove zero service calls when specialty is missing.
Tests separate draft edits and display defaults without claiming screen coverage.
questions.answerHTML:
Make load(draft:service:) return a named state. First check that specialty exists. If it is missing, return the selection-required state before calling the service. Otherwise use do/catch: every successful list, even [], becomes loaded. Known offline failure becomes retry guidance; handle unexpected errors deliberately too. Missing procedure remains allowed and must not turn into a made-up ID.

Use a deterministic fake configured with a result and a spy that records calls. A validation test should assert both the failure state and zero service calls; merely observing the message does not prove the ordering. Separate tests check independent draft edits, the empty-query display rule, empty success versus offline, and nonempty result preservation. Use Swift Testing or XCTest consistently within each test. These synchronous host tests establish the model boundary's behavior. They do not establish cancellation, localization, rendering, or any real network behavior that the lab does not implement.
followUps: Why does checking the whole state protect more than checking the number of names?
What new rule would you need for queries containing only whitespace?
pitfalls: Testing returned names while leaving offline behavior unchecked.
Assuming a final validation message proves the service was never called.

questions.prompt: Do these tests detect the broken error handling? Explain what must be asserted when do/catch is replaced by try? and an empty-list fallback.
questions.scenario: The made-up load function is deliberately changed to loaded((try? service.search(for: draft)) ?? []). Its tests still pass: for both offline and no matches, they only check that the result has zero elements.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin tests that assert list size after runCatching.getOrDefault(emptyList()) have the same blind spot. Swift enum equality compares the represented state when Equatable conformance is available; this is a behavioral assertion, not a guarantee supplied by the test framework itself.
rubric: Explains how the fallback changes offline into successful empty data.
Checks expected final states rather than only list counts.
Runs the deliberate change to show that the strengthened test detects it.
Names behavior outside the model lab that passing tests cannot prove.
questions.answerHTML:
The broken version keeps the same count but changes what the count means. Offline becomes loaded([]), so checking zero names cannot tell failure from successful no matches. Check the whole expected state for each fixture, meaning a known test input. The empty-success fixture should produce loaded with no names. The offline fixture should produce the agreed failed state. Check that those outcomes differ.

Run the deliberate mutation against those expectations: the offline assertion should fail for the lost retry behavior. Restore explicit error mapping after inspecting that failure. This checks that the test detects a product distinction rather than reproducing private branch structure. Keep fixtures deterministic and independent of real requests. A passing suite still leaves requirements such as whitespace normalization, localized messages, and later asynchronous cancellation unverified. If callbacks are introduced, their lifetime and captures need a fresh review. Neither the mutation exercise nor reading its worked solution establishes the learner's own execution results.
followUps: What deliberate change would reveal a missing specialty-validation test?
If message strings no longer express enough detail, how would you preserve typed failure reasons?
pitfalls: Changing test expectations to accept the deliberately broken behavior.
Calling successful compilation a completed test run.

questions.prompt: What happens for empty success, offline failure, and a saved callback called after its owner is released? Explain the state and lifetime rules together.
questions.scenario: ReviewOwner stores a refresh callback using weak self and calls a protocol service that can throw. Save the callback elsewhere and invoke it. Then clear the outside owner variable and invoke the saved callback again.
questions.androidBridge: Android sealed outcomes and an injected interface support the same separation of empty success from failure. Kotlin callback storage can retain an owner, but JVM garbage collection and Swift ARC have different cycle behavior; weak capture does not implement a LifecycleOwner-style stop policy.
rubric: Predicts no matches for loaded([]) and retry for offline.
Separates how long the saved closure lives from how long its owner lives.
Explains guard let self and safe return when the owner is missing.
Distinguishes safe object access from permission to update a screen whose flow has ended.
questions.answerHTML:
The first call checks that the weak owner still exists, then asks the service for names. Empty success becomes loaded with an empty list and displays no matches. Offline takes the error path and displays retry. Neither outcome has names to display, but they mean different things. An exhaustive summary, which handles every state case, keeps their next actions separate.

The saved variable strongly owns the closure, but the closure's weak capture does not own ReviewOwner. Once every other strong owner is removed, the weak probe can become nil. Calling the saved closure then reaches its absent-owner guard and returns safely. The local self created by successful unwrapping temporarily owns the instance during use. Because the initializer constructs a stored closure directly, there is no incoming plain closure parameter requiring an escaping annotation. Finally, ownership safety does not establish lifecycle correctness: an owner retained elsewhere may still be alive after its flow ends, so asynchronous extensions would need an explicit update and cancellation policy.
followUps: What annotation is needed if an initializer accepts a plain callback parameter and stores it?
What links would a nested stored callback add to the ownership graph?
pitfalls: Assuming a saved closure keeps its weak owner alive.
Treating a successful weak-reference check as permission to update any screen state.

questions.prompt: For each review finding, name a separate diagnostic plan and the evidence it needs. Why is one compiler-version explanation insufficient?
questions.scenario: A made-up walkthrough finds three issues: an implementation does not meet its protocol, an imported module is unavailable, and a test target compiles with no run result. A reviewer blames the installed compiler version for all three.
questions.androidBridge: Android signature checking, Gradle module resolution, and JUnit discovery are separate diagnostic boundaries too. Swift tools declarations and Xcode scheme actions have their own roles; a Kotlin compiler or Gradle version analogy does not determine another Swift target's effective language mode.
rubric: Compares method labels, types, results, and effects with the protocol requirement.
Checks dependency, platform, and source inclusion for the missing import.
Checks test conventions and the selected test action for execution.
Separates facts read from source, predictions, and saved results from actual runs.
questions.answerHTML:
Check each failure where it occurs. For protocol conformance, meaning meeting the protocol's promise, compare the method name, argument labels, input and result types, and throws or async effects. For a missing module, inspect the consumer's target, dependency, exported product, import name, platform, and source inclusion. For tests that compile but have not run, check framework discovery and the scheme's test action, then obtain a run artifact.

The installed compiler alone cannot settle any of those questions. Its version differs from manifest tools requirements, effective language mode, SDK, and deployment target. Write the selected build route beside each finding. In the walkthrough, keep source-visible facts separate from predicted consequences and checks you have executed. A verified source glob supports membership; a test result supports execution; an isolated program supports only its own language and ownership behavior. A useful handoff names the narrow next check and its expected evidence rather than promising that regeneration will fix every category.
followUps: What evidence would distinguish an async requirement mismatch from a missing-module problem?
How would you describe an ownership risk found in source before reproducing it?
pitfalls: Using a neighboring target's build settings as evidence for this target.
Calling a test file's presence a passing test result.

questions.prompt: Why is the counter still two after returning from detail? Explain why a screen disappearing does not prove its controller was released or its work should end.
questions.scenario: A made-up UIKit counter reaches two, pushes a detail controller, then becomes visible again. Logs show one initial view load and several appearance events. A presentation can also cover the counter.
questions.androidBridge: Android Activity and Fragment callbacks used from Kotlin or Java help separate setup from repeated visibility. UIKit controller ownership, view loading, containment, and scene activity are distinct mechanisms; viewDidDisappear is not an exact onDestroy or terminal onStop equivalent.
rubric: Explains why the navigation stack retains the counter controller.
Separates controller creation, view loading, appearance, layout, and release.
Sets up the view hierarchy once without resetting stored state on each appearance.
Looks for actual removal or dismissal before reporting that the flow ended.
questions.answerHTML:
The navigation stack still owns the counter controller while detail is shown. Returning reveals that same controller, whose stored count is two. It need not build its views again. Put one-time view construction in the loading path. Decide separately whether each return should refresh data. Visibility tells you what is shown; ownership tells you what stays alive.

Controller initialization, view loading, appearance, layout, scene activity, and deallocation describe different events. Accessing the view can load it without making it visible. Layout and appearance callbacks can repeat. Disappearance can mean coverage, a transition, or removal, so it does not by itself justify reporting cancellation. Inspect the navigation or presentation event that ends the flow. A popped controller may still have another strong owner, and a retaining task may delay deallocation. Use deinit as lifetime evidence after auditing owners, while performing timely cleanup at the explicit stopping event required by the feature.
followUps: Where would you install constraints so returning does not activate duplicates?
What would prove that the pushed controller was removed from the stack?
pitfalls: Resetting model state each time the controller appears.
Treating viewDidDisappear as deinit or as the scene entering the background.

questions.prompt: How should UIKit attach and remove a hosted SwiftUI child? Explain the controller relationship and any separate references that keep it alive.
questions.scenario: A parent calls addSubview(host.view) and keeps host in a property. Later it removes the view. It has no clear controller-attachment or property-cleanup policy, and layout and appearance behave inconsistently.
questions.androidBridge: Adding an Android View is not equivalent to attaching a Fragment with its manager and lifecycle. Similarly, adding UIHostingController.view establishes only a view relationship; UIKit child-controller containment needs its own notifications and ownership, beyond any ComposeView analogy.
rubric: Attaches with addChild, view insertion and constraints, then didMove(toParent:).
Removes with willMove(toParent: nil), view removal, then removeFromParent.
Clears separately owned references and constraints when the parent's policy ends their lifetime.
Explains why adding the view alone does not establish controller containment.
questions.answerHTML:
A hosting controller has two relationships to manage: its view belongs in the view tree, and the controller belongs in the controller tree. Adding only its view establishes the first. In the main-actor UI context, call parent.addChild(host), insert and constrain its view, then call host.didMove(toParent: parent). addChild already sends the incoming willMove notification.

For removal, call host.willMove(toParent: nil), remove the root view and any separately managed constraints, then host.removeFromParent(). Clear the parent's separate property when its ownership should end; otherwise the child can remain retained even after proper removal. Investigate the actual hierarchy and callback sequence rather than attributing every symptom to SwiftUI rendering. Verify both re-embedding and teardown in a scratch target. This plan explains containment and lifetime, but does not claim a particular appearance failure has been reproduced on a device.
followUps: Who keeps a factory-created hosting controller alive when attachment is the caller's job?
What references would you inspect if a weak probe still sees it after removal?
pitfalls: Treating addSubview as complete child-controller attachment.
Expecting view removal to clear a separate strong property.

questions.prompt: Who stores the observable draft, who edits it, and who only reads it? Explain the jobs of State, Binding, Bindable, and a plain model property.
questions.scenario: An iOS 17+ root creates an @Observable draft isolated to MainActor. One child edits name with TextField. Another displays canContinue. Unrelated root updates should keep the same draft.
questions.androidBridge: Compose remembered state and state hoisting are useful analogies for SwiftUI identity-associated State and passed bindings. SwiftUI View values are descriptions rather than retained Android View objects; Observation tracks property reads and does not equal StateFlow, persistence, or a ViewModel lifetime.
rubric: Uses root State to preserve the locally created model for stable identity.
Uses Bindable when the editing child needs projected bindings.
Lets the read-only child track model reads through a plain property.
Separates observing changes, MainActor isolation, model ownership, and saving data.
questions.answerHTML:
@State connects the root's locally owned draft to storage for a stable SwiftUI identity. Identity is how SwiftUI recognizes the same place in the interface across new view descriptions. @Binding gives a child read and write access to another owner's value. @Bindable supplies editing bindings such as $draft.name for an observable model; it does not create a second draft.

A read-only child can receive a plain model property and read name or computed canContinue in its body. Observation tracks those property dependencies; it does not require that child to own the model. @MainActor separately controls where those properties may be changed. Neither annotation persists the draft, restores a process, or defines logout cleanup. Keeping identity stable preserves local state, while intentionally replacing identity can reset it. These examples require supported Observation integration and do not replace the older ObservableObject wrappers used by other lesson examples.
followUps: Why calculate canContinue instead of keeping a separate validity flag in sync?
Which wrappers would you use for an externally owned legacy ObservableObject?
pitfalls: Treating Bindable as ownership or disk storage.
Expecting @Observable to make arbitrary concurrent edits safe.

questions.prompt: Why can the editor keep record A's draft after receiving record B? Choose how records change without losing unsaved typing.
questions.scenario: An editor initializes State from a record argument. The parent later supplies another record but keeps the editor's identity. A proposed fix adds a new random UUID every time body runs; typing now disappears.
questions.androidBridge: Compose remember(initialInput) keys can help reason about deliberate resets, but SwiftUI uses its own hierarchy and explicit identity rules. Neither remembered state nor State automatically follows every changed constructor argument or survives process death without a separate restoration mechanism.
rubric: Explains that initialization seeds storage for a new identity.
Identifies a changing random identity as the reason typing resets.
Chooses parent ownership, explicit replacement, or stable record identity with an unsaved-edit rule.
Tests unrelated updates, record switches, and explicit Reset separately.
questions.answerHTML:
State takes its initial value when SwiftUI creates storage for an identity. A new initializer argument does not necessarily replace existing storage at that same identity. Thus A's unsaved draft can remain after the parent supplies B. This can protect edits, but it conflicts with an editor meant to switch records. Decide who owns replacement and what happens to unsaved work.

Choose an explicit contract: have the parent own the active draft, implement a replace-record operation with unsaved-edit handling, or use a stable record-based identity when a record switch should create a fresh editor. A random UUID on every render repeatedly destroys local state and explains the erased typing. Test that an unrelated parent change preserves edits, that switching records follows the chosen confirmation or reset rule, and that explicit Reset behaves independently. Keep model initialization free of required side effects because description construction can create candidate instances without replacing existing storage. Persistence remains a separate requirement.
followUps: How would you preserve separate unsaved drafts for several records?
How does replacing identity differ from changing fields on the existing draft?
pitfalls: Expecting each initializer argument change to overwrite State.
Forcing updates with random identity while ignoring destroyed state.

questions.prompt: How should a SwiftUI wrapper create, update, and remove its UIKit controller? How does its delegate call the latest onEdit callback?
questions.scenario: UIKitMessage receives changing message text and an onEdit closure. Keep the represented controller's identity stable. Its delegate must use the current callback, even after SwiftUI creates a new wrapper description.
questions.androidBridge: Compose AndroidView's factory and update responsibilities resemble a representable's make and update methods. SwiftUI's representable Coordinator has framework-specific lifetime and delegate duties; it is not automatically a navigation coordinator, Fragment, or coroutine scope.
rubric: Creates in make and applies changed inputs in update.
Uses a stable representable coordinator for delegate callbacks.
Refreshes the coordinator's callback or binding as inputs change.
Removes only bridge-owned work and avoids reporting synchronization as a user edit.
questions.answerHTML:
makeUIViewController creates the UIKit controller for this represented identity. updateUIViewController passes current SwiftUI inputs to that same controller. For example, changing a message from Ready to Saved should update its label rather than rebuild the controller. If the display method needs loaded views, deliberately load the hierarchy before assigning the text.

The representable's coordinator carries delegate and callback integration across temporary wrapper values. Update its current closure or binding when inputs change; retaining the initial wrapper forever can deliver edits to obsolete state. Compare existing and incoming text before assignment when unnecessary writes would disturb selection or focus, and avoid treating a state synchronization as a new user edit. Teardown can detach delegates and cancel subscriptions owned by this bridge, with an explicit lifetime policy. It must not cancel a shared operation merely because one wrapper disappears. The representable coordinator solves interoperability lifetime, while navigation ownership and hosted-controller containment remain separate decisions.
followUps: When is an empty update method valid?
What observation would separate an old callback from an old label value?
pitfalls: Creating a new controller for every input change.
Keeping the first callback after its intended destination changes.

questions.prompt: For each way the picker can end, say what result it returns and who stops lookup work. Why do no search matches and invalid starting input need different handling?
questions.scenario: A picker can select, cancel, be popped with Back, or be swiped away as a modal. Searches may find no matches. It has optional lookup work and a weak presentation delegate. An empty initial data set breaks the caller's input contract.
questions.androidBridge: Android navigation results and dialog dismissal callbacks raise similar finish-once and cleanup questions. UIKit pushed removal and presentation-controller delegation are distinct paths; Swift weak delegate storage does not supply the delegate adapter's lifetime, unlike assuming callback registration retains an Android listener.
rubric: Returns a selected value for selection and cancellation for terminal user exits.
Leaves the picker active after a search with no matches.
Handles invalid initial input through invocation recovery.
Names who retains the delegate adapter, prevents duplicate finish calls, and cleans lookup work on each exit.
questions.answerHTML:
List the outcomes first. Selection returns a chosen value. Cancel, completed back removal, and interactive modal dismissal return cancellation. No search matches leaves the picker open for another query. Invalid starting input is different: the caller violated this picker's input contract, so use its diagnostic and alert recovery path. Do not present that mistake as a successful search with no matches.

Each terminal path must identify who delivers the result and stops optional lookup work. Retain the dismissal adapter elsewhere because a weak delegate reference cannot keep it alive. Disable competing removal callbacks during an explicit selected-result transition and preserve the finish-once caller contract even if result storage rejects duplicates. The lesson identifies different lookup-cleanup paths in source; that is a concrete review question, not observed runtime harm. Verify with controlled pending work and focused navigation integration checks. A direct delegate invocation establishes callback handling but does not prove an actual swipe gesture completed.
followUps: Why might accepting only the first result still leave cleanup unfinished?
How would you test lookup completion after the picker is popped?
pitfalls: Ending the picker whenever search finds no matches.
Expecting a weak delegate property to keep its adapter alive.

questions.prompt: Why can an old request still change a MainActor model after await? Explain the request checks needed before publishing either success or failure.
questions.scenario: Request A waits. B starts and finishes. Then A succeeds or fails. The model publishes loading, loaded, failed, or idle. Its agreed rule is that canceling the current request returns the screen to idle.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin suspend functions also suspend without inherently selecting a background dispatcher. MainActor resembles a declared UI isolation domain, while Dispatchers.Main familiarity does not imply atomicity across suspension. A canceled coroutine or Swift task can require cooperative checks and a separate freshness policy.
rubric: Explains await as possible suspension and interleaving, not automatic background work.
Captures the request revision before waiting.
Checks current revision in both success and failure paths.
Distinguishes cancellation from service failure and applies the chosen UI rule only to the current request.
questions.answerHTML:
MainActor protects access to the model's UI state, but waiting lets other work run. While A is suspended at await, B can become the current request. Give each request a revision, a value identifying which request is current. Capture it before waiting. After the service returns, check both cancellation and the revision before publishing loaded, even if the service ignored cancellation.

Perform the same freshness comparison in the catch path. Otherwise A's late error or cancellation can replace B's newer loaded result with failed or idle. Only the current request may apply the model's cancellation policy; this example chooses idle, while another feature could retain earlier content. Classify cancellation using the task state and the service's documented cancellation behavior rather than assuming every API throws the same error type. The async keyword does not guarantee off-main work, and actor isolation does not preserve pre-await assumptions. Use controlled A/B completions to verify both late success and late failure.
followUps: How would keeping earlier content change the current-request cancellation rule?
Why is checking cancellation only before the service call insufficient?
pitfalls: Treating MainActor as a lock held through the whole async method.
Rejecting old successes but letting old failures erase newer results.

questions.prompt: Why does the inner Task keep running after the view task changes? Explain where to await the load and who should own any deliberately separate task.
questions.scenario: A screen uses .task(id: query) { Task { await model.load(id: query) } }. Fast query changes leave old loads running. Leaving the screen sometimes displays an unavailable error.
questions.androidBridge: Compose LaunchedEffect(key) is a useful conceptual neighbor of .task(id:), but creating independently owned coroutine work can also escape the expected scope. Swift Task braces create unstructured work; lexical nesting does not make it a coroutineScope-style structured child.
rubric: Identifies the inner Task as unstructured work with separate ownership.
Awaits the async load directly from the view-associated task.
Explains that cancellation is cooperative and dropping a handle does not cancel work.
Keeps current-request checks and an explicit rule for displaying cancellation.
questions.answerHTML:
The view's .task(id:) owns associated work and requests cancellation when the ID changes or its lifetime ends. The inner Task creates unstructured work with a separate lifetime. Being written inside the outer task does not make it a managed child. Await the model load directly inside the modifier so that the load runs within the view-associated task.

If a synchronous event legitimately launches unstructured work, assign a feature owner, retain its handle, and cancel it at the defined stopping event. Dropping the handle is not cancellation, and weak capture only changes object ownership. Cancellation remains cooperative: check it after suspension and avoid mapping it to an ordinary unavailable error. Keep request revisions because old work may finish before or despite cancellation. Verify replacement and disappearance with a controlled service, including an old error after a new success. This reasoning defines a task and presentation contract, without asserting that a real transport stopped on a device.
followUps: When should work continue after the view disappears, and who should own it?
What should happen if a fake ignores cancellation and later returns?
pitfalls: Expecting lexical nesting to give Task a structured child lifetime.
Using weak self instead of cancellation and current-request checks.

questions.prompt: Design tests that control when cancellation and overlapping requests happen. How does canceling before work starts differ from canceling while the service waits?
questions.scenario: A model uses an injectable async service. Its current test creates a Task and immediately cancels it. A proposed overlap test waits ten milliseconds before starting request B.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin coroutine test schedulers and controlled fakes help establish ordering rather than wall-clock luck. Swift Task.yield and sleep are not equivalents of runTest's scheduling controls; XCTest expectations or explicit async signals must encode the event you need to observe.
rubric: States the limited behavior covered by immediate cancellation.
Waits for an explicit fake start signal before canceling or replacing work.
Finishes B before A and tests both A's late success and late failure.
Awaits task completion and releases every pending fake operation.
questions.answerHTML:
Immediate cancellation can test work that begins already canceled. It cannot prove the service had started waiting. Give the fake service a start signal and a completion gate, which holds its answer until the test releases it. Start the load, wait for the signal, request cancellation, open the gate, and await the owning task. Then check the agreed state, including when the fake ignores cancellation.

For freshness, start A and observe its gate, then start B and observe B's gate. Complete B and establish its loaded result before completing A. Assert that A's late success cannot overwrite B; repeat with A failing to check the catch guard. A sleep or yield cannot establish these events reliably. Use the appropriate actor isolation for the model and asynchronous XCTest fulfillment when callback evidence is needed. Ensure every gate is released and every task is joined so no work mutates state after the assertion or hangs the test.
followUps: What would fail if the catch path lost its current-request check?
Why could a blocking MainActor wait prevent the event it is waiting for?
pitfalls: Using a longer sleep as proof of event order.
Leaving fake operations waiting after assertions finish.

questions.prompt: A toolchain update changed a snapshot. How should you review it, and what separate checks are needed for returned results, swipe dismissal, and accessibility?
questions.scenario: A picker image differs after a toolchain update. One teammate wants to record every new baseline. Another says a stable UI identifier and a direct dismissal-delegate test prove both accessibility and swipe behavior.
questions.androidBridge: Android screenshot tests and Espresso-style interaction checks also answer different questions. SnapshotTesting is a third-party iOS library, while XCUIApplication operates across an app boundary; neither is a direct substitute for model assertions or a complete TalkBack or VoiceOver task review.
rubric: Reviews images and rendering conditions before recording a new baseline.
Separates visual comparison from checks of the coordinator's returned result.
Distinguishes calling a delegate from performing the actual gesture.
Explains why an automation identifier does not prove spoken labels or accessible task completion.
questions.answerHTML:
A snapshot is an image captured under chosen conditions and compared with an accepted baseline. Compare both images before accepting a change. Check the fixture, fonts, layout timing, dimensions, appearance, scale, OS, and SDK. Decide whether the difference is intended UI behavior or changed rendering. Recording a baseline needs review; raising tolerance may simply hide a real regression.

A snapshot establishes a visual contract under those conditions. A coordinator test establishes the selected or cancelled result, while a focused UI test can verify app-level navigation and an actual gesture. Invoking the presentation delegate directly checks callback integration but does not perform UIKit's swipe transition. A stable accessibility identifier supports automation lookup; it does not establish labels, focus order, or task completion with VoiceOver. Choose the narrow additional evidence for the changed requirement, and label unexecuted checks as planned. One phone-size snapshot cannot establish large-text, localization, or tablet behavior.
followUps: When should you add a large-text snapshot as well as updating the default image?
How would you provide deterministic app data for XCUIApplication?
pitfalls: Recording every changed image merely to make tests pass.
Claiming an identifier or direct delegate call proves the full interaction.

questions.prompt: Describe one booking draft shared by the editor, reason picker, and Review. Explain validation, selection, Cancel, Reset, UIKit updates, and load lifetime.
questions.scenario: The app collects displayName and optional reason, shows a reason picker, pushes Review, embeds UIKitMessage, and loads a made-up review result. Returning preserves edits. Reset clears fields without replacing navigation.
questions.androidBridge: One hoisted Compose state holder or Android UI-state owner resembles this shared draft boundary. SwiftUI Observation and identity-associated State have different mechanics from StateFlow or ViewModel; a modal NavigationStack is a separate presentation scope rather than a second copy of the draft.
rubric: Defines one MainActor observable draft with optional selection and calculated canReview.
Rejects whitespace-only names without a separate mutable validity flag.
Shares the root-owned model with picker and Review.
Separates field Reset, navigation state, UIKit updates, and review-load lifetime.
questions.answerHTML:
Give the draft one owner. Use a MainActor observable model with a name, optional reason, calculated canReview, and reset(). Calculate eligibility from a trimmed nonempty name and a present reason. A second mutable validity flag could disagree with the fields. The root keeps this model in State; picker and Review receive the same object. Editing controls use bindings to its fields.

A selection writes the chosen reason and dismisses the picker. Cancel only dismisses, preserving any existing choice. Review navigation leaves the root owner intact, so returning keeps the draft. Reset clears fields explicitly without randomly changing identity or replacing the stack. Apply current review text through the UIKit bridge's update method and give the synthetic load a view-associated task. Validate fields with model tests, then check picker cancellation, navigation return, bridge sizing, and task behavior at their actual integration boundaries.
followUps: What should happen when the user chooses the same reason twice?
Why should Reset avoid assigning a random identity to the root?
pitfalls: Giving picker and Review independent drafts.
Keeping validity, presentation, and navigation flags without rules preventing contradictions.

questions.prompt: Why does Cancel change the old reason, and why does the UIKit message stay old? Trace each issue to its own handoff and test the intended behavior.
questions.scenario: The picker writes each highlighted row into the committed draft before confirmation. Cancel only dismisses. Review sees the shared model correctly, but UIKitMessage has an empty updateUIViewController method.
questions.androidBridge: Android dialogs with provisional state can also corrupt committed selections if they write too early. Compose AndroidView updates offer a similar bridge checkpoint, but SwiftUI representable updates and scoped dismissal follow their own lifecycle; reactive model observation alone does not update a UIKit label.
rubric: Identifies that highlighting commits before the cancellation decision.
Chooses either immediate selection or local tentative state with explicit confirmation.
Applies current text through updateUIViewController.
Tests Cancel with a previous reason and message changes on the same controller.
questions.answerHTML:
A highlighted row is a tentative choice unless the interaction says selection commits immediately. Here it already changes the shared draft, so Cancel cannot simply dismiss and preserve the old reason. Choose a consistent rule: immediate selection commits and closes, as in the lab, or local tentative selection commits only on Confirm. With local selection, Cancel discards it. Test both absent and existing previous choices.

The stale UIKit message has a different cause. Observation can cause SwiftUI to recompute the wrapper, but an empty update method never applies the new input to its retained controller. Implement update to call the controller's display method with the current message, loading its hierarchy if necessary. Verify that the same controller identity displays the changed value. Record model events, presentation changes, and bridge updates separately to establish the causal chain. Random identity resets could hide both symptoms while destroying the draft, so they do not satisfy the stated contract.
followUps: What event log would show Cancel kept the committed reason?
If the message changes but the row has zero height, what would you inspect?
pitfalls: Writing tentative highlights into shared state before defining Cancel.
Expecting Observation alone to configure the embedded UIKit view.

questions.prompt: Trace one picker action from caller input to returned result. Explain composition, state, rendering, navigation, and ownership, and say what source inspection can prove.
questions.scenario: Compare the visit-reason picker walkthrough with the address form. You can read linked source and tests. You have no saved app run or device observations.
questions.androidBridge: Tracing an Android feature through navigation, ViewModel, repository, and tests provides a useful investigation habit. Swift coordinators, hosted-controller containment, weak delegates, and Observation differ in ownership; a familiar architecture name cannot replace checking the actual iOS integration contract.
rubric: Begins with public input, output, presentation, and caller obligations.
Separates what each part does from its strong and weak references.
Follows query changes, selection events, navigation, and final result.
Labels source facts, conditional risks, planned checks, and actual run evidence.
questions.answerHTML:
Start with the caller's promise: accepted input, selected or canceled output, presentation choices, isolation, and who must keep the flow alive. Follow the wrapper into the UIKit host, coordinator, observable model, displayed view, delegate, and result delivery. Composition means assembling these parts. Draw strong owners and weak references separately. Calling another part does not necessarily keep it alive.

Trace a query edit into derived rows, then selection through the model delegate into the navigation transition and finish call. Include back removal, modal dismissal, invalid input, and nonterminal no matches. Compare the address form's caller-owned hosted containment rather than assuming the same coordinator owns everything. Map model, coordinator, snapshot, and UI tests to the requirements they express. Source and test inspection support facts about declarations and intended coverage, not executed results. Write conditional risks with their assumptions and name the check that would resolve them. This produces a review another engineer can verify without claiming a device run.
followUps: How can a weak hosting-controller property still refer to a visible retained screen?
How does a finish-once caller promise differ from defensive rejection of duplicate results?
pitfalls: Starting with wrappers while missing the caller's contract.
Reporting test source as evidence that the tests ran successfully.

questions.prompt: The two exit paths clean up differently. What does the source show, what remains unproven, and what small test would establish the consequence?
questions.scenario: Explicit pop calls fetchTask.cancel() before finish. Pushed removal calls finish(.cancelled) directly. Base finish accepts the first result but does not cancel subclass task properties. No harmful runtime behavior has been observed.
questions.androidBridge: Android navigation result completion does not necessarily cancel a separately launched coroutine either. Swift's coordinator finish and unstructured Task ownership are distinct contracts; first-result protection is not a LifecycleScope-style automatic cleanup mechanism.
rubric: States the source-observed difference without claiming a reproduced defect.
Defines whether every terminal path should stop optional lookup.
Uses a start signal and controlled late completion after pushed removal.
Checks result count, allowed updates, and eventual work cleanup.
questions.answerHTML:
The source shows a difference: explicit pop requests lookup cancellation; pushed removal directly returns cancellation. The base finish method prevents duplicate results but does not manage the subclass's tasks. Those are separate jobs. This is evidence of different cleanup paths, not proof of a leak or a bad update. First decide whether optional lookup should stop whenever the flow ends.

Define whether optional suggestions should stop on every terminal path. Use a fake lookup that signals start and waits behind a gate. Start the flow, wait for that signal, trigger the pushed-removal path, then inspect cancellation state and release the lookup with success or failure. Assert the agreed no-update behavior, exactly one cancelled result, and eventual work cleanup. A helper-level test can isolate callbacks; a focused UI path is needed if actual gesture and container integration are the uncertain part. Explain any remaining ownership that keeps the model alive and report the test as planned until it executes.
followUps: What if finish rejects duplicate results but lookup still runs?
What separate check would establish actual interactive removal?
pitfalls: Calling a source difference a confirmed production incident.
Assuming finish automatically cancels every task in the subclass.

questions.prompt: When should you use async let and when should you use a throwing task group? Keep list results in input order, allow at most three active loads, and return no partial array on failure.
questions.scenario: A dashboard needs two fixed independent loads. Another operation receives any number of IDs. It must return values in the same order as those IDs, keep at most three loads in flight, and fail as a whole if a load fails.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin coroutineScope with async children resembles structured Swift async let and task-group ownership. Swift task groups yield completion order and are not a direct supervisorScope counterpart; catching child failures deliberately changes whether partial success is allowed.
rubric: Chooses async let for the fixed pair and a group for varying input.
Returns input indices with child values and changes output only in the parent.
Starts at most three children and adds one when a completion frees a slot.
Explains cancellation and waiting for children when an error escapes the group.
questions.answerHTML:
Use async let for the two known independent dashboard loads, then await both to build the dashboard. A task group fits a list whose length varies. Have each child return its input index and value. Children finish in any order, so the parent uses the index to place each result correctly. Only the parent changes the output array; the children do not share mutable output.

Seed at most three children and submit one new input after each completion frees a slot. Empty input starts none. If an error escapes the group body, remaining children are cancelled and joined, and the function throws instead of returning a partial array. Catching each child into Result would intentionally define another policy. Structured scope exit waits for its children; cancellation is cooperative rather than forced termination. The window bounds active loads, not total result memory or requests per second. Verify ordering, peak activity, failure, and cancellation with explicit fake gates.
followUps: Why can three active loads still exceed a requests-per-second limit?
How would allowing partial success change results and error handling?
pitfalls: Returning completion order when input order was promised.
Submitting every input at once and calling the load bounded.

questions.prompt: Why can a task-group timeout still return after its deadline? Explain how cancellation reaches the callback source and how the continuation finishes exactly once.
questions.scenario: A callback operation is wrapped in a checked continuation. The timeout child wins and cancels siblings, but the callback source ignores cancellation. The caller expects the group to return immediately at the deadline.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin withTimeout also relies on cooperation and cannot forcibly terminate arbitrary blocking work. Swift group scope additionally joins its children; CheckedContinuation is a one-result bridge, not an automatic cancellation-aware replacement for suspendCancellableCoroutine.
rubric: Explains why group exit waits for canceled children to finish.
Separates reaching the deadline from forcibly stopping the underlying source.
Connects cancellation to the source and synchronizes exactly-once continuation completion.
Tests cancellation and completion in both orders and states any remaining deadline limit.
questions.answerHTML:
The task timeout chooses a result but cannot force the other child to finish. A transport timeout is a separate mechanism. A task group waits for its children when its scope ends, including canceled children. If a callback source keeps waiting, the group can remain open after the deadline. A checked continuation bridges one callback result into an async wait. It does not automatically stop the callback source when cancellation is requested.

Define how the bridge cancels its underlying operation and how the continuation completes when cancellation races a normal callback. A checked continuation must resume exactly once; a cancellation handler may run concurrently, so protect the completion state with a suitable synchronized mechanism rather than an unsafely shared Boolean. If the source cannot be stopped, the design must state that limitation and assign an owner to any work that continues independently. Test completion-before-cancellation and cancellation-before-completion using gates, then join every task. Do not recover by swallowing cancellation into an empty success or by promising a hard deadline that the dependency cannot honor.
followUps: What can defer do if cleanup itself needs an async wait?
When would a transport timeout give stronger deadline evidence than this race?
pitfalls: Expecting cancelAll to forcibly stop callback work.
Resuming from both cancellation and completion without protecting shared completion state.

questions.prompt: What happens when reset runs while an actor load waits? Explain why this contract must reject the old result for both the cache and the waiting caller.
questions.scenario: SnapshotStore starts loading. While it waits, reset increments the account generation and clears the cache. The loader ignores cancellation and returns later. The contract rejects old-account success, not just old cache insertion.
questions.androidBridge: An actor serializes isolated state access, whereas a Kotlin Mutex held across a suspend call can exclude other holders for the whole critical section. Swift actor methods permit interleaving at suspension; neither actors nor mutexes alone define account ownership, caller outcomes, or distributed transactions.
rubric: Identifies reset as allowed work during the load's suspension.
Captures generation before waiting and checks it after cancellation handling.
Rejects old success for the caller as well as preventing cache insertion.
Names a separate policy for overlapping loads in the same generation.
questions.answerHTML:
An actor controls access to its state in separate turns. It does not hold one turn throughout an async wait. Reset can therefore run while load is suspended. Capture the account generation, the number identifying this ownership period, before waiting. After return, check cancellation and that number before committing. If it changed, throw account-changed and keep the cache empty. Keep the final check and cache update in one turn without another await.

This store rejects old success for the waiting caller too. A generalized cache might instead return an old result while refusing insertion; that is a different contract that must not be copied accidentally. Cancellation reduces wasted work, while generation validation preserves correctness even if the loader ignores it. Two concurrent loads in the same generation can still finish in either order, so this simple store does not establish latest-request-wins or coalescing. Add those policies explicitly when callers need them. Actor safety also does not override a disk framework's confinement rules or establish a transaction with a server.
followUps: Why is the same account string after A → B → A insufficient?
How would you test the caller's failure separately from the cache remaining empty?
pitfalls: Calling actor isolation a transaction held across await.
Rejecting cache insertion but returning old-account data as current success.

questions.prompt: Is this struct safe to pass between tasks? Explain why @unchecked Sendable and nonisolated do not repair unprotected mutable state.
questions.scenario: A struct stores let notes: MutableNotes, a class whose fields can change. A teammate adds @unchecked Sendable to silence transfer diagnostics and marks an actor accessor nonisolated even though it reads mutable actor state.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin val holding a mutable object does not make that object immutable or thread-safe, just as Swift let does not. Kotlin has no exact compiler-enforced Sendable counterpart; mutex or dispatcher conventions cannot justify a Swift unchecked annotation without a documented synchronization invariant.
rubric: Identifies the mutable object inside the let field.
Distinguishes Sendable values from @Sendable closure capture rules.
Explains that unchecked conformance supplies no synchronization.
Rejects nonisolated reads of mutable actor state and proposes a safe snapshot or isolated owner.
questions.answerHTML:
The struct copies its field values, but its notes field still points to a mutable object. let fixes which object is referenced; it does not freeze the object's text. Use an immutable snapshot made of safely transferable values, or let an actor own and control mutable notes. Actor references can cross isolation boundaries safely because access to isolated members still follows the actor's rules.

Sendable promises safe transfer of values. @Sendable constrains closure captures, the values a closure remembers, and their use. @unchecked Sendable is a manual promise and adds no lock, so it needs a complete documented protection mechanism that the compiler cannot establish. Marking an accessor nonisolated opts it out of actor isolation; it cannot thereby safely read arbitrary mutable isolated state. Return a snapshot through an isolated operation instead. Likewise, referencing a MainActor model from another domain does not permit synchronous mutation of its UI properties. Diagnose the ownership and access invariant rather than suppressing the diagnostic.
followUps: How could a shared mutable test counter make an @Sendable fake unsafe?
When can a genuinely immutable property support a nonisolated API?
pitfalls: Treating let as deep immutability and automatic transfer safety.
Using unchecked or nonisolated as if either added a lock.

questions.prompt: What does bufferingNewest(1) keep or drop? Why can it suit progress but damage required text fragments, and why doesn't it slow the producer?
questions.scenario: A callback source emits progress faster than one consumer processes it. AsyncStream uses bufferingNewest(1). Another team wants the same factory for ordered text fragments and expects slow iteration to make production wait.
questions.androidBridge: Kotlin Flow, StateFlow, and channels help distinguish collection, replaceable state, and required events. AsyncSequence does not imply cold Flow behavior or multicast, and continuation-based AsyncStream.yield does not suspend the producer like a suspending channel send.
rubric: Explains the one waiting newest value and possible loss of older buffered values.
Separates a bounded buffer from making production wait.
Allows replacement for complete progress state but preserves required text fragments.
Defines consumer count, start and stop rules, and a payload-size limit.
questions.answerHTML:
bufferingNewest(1) keeps at most one waiting value. A newer progress update can replace an older buffered update. That works when each value fully describes current progress and skipped intermediate states are allowed. It does not make the producer wait: continuation yield reports whether a value was enqueued, dropped, or the stream ended. Limiting a buffer and applying producer backpressure are different promises.

Ordered text fragments may depend on every earlier fragment, so dropping them can corrupt the output. Use complete cumulative snapshots or a producer-consumer protocol that explicitly provides backpressure and required-event handling. A one-element bound also does not bound bytes if an element can be enormous. Define production start time, consumer count, overflow, failure, and stopping behavior. Constructing a stream can start its producer before iteration, and one AsyncStream is not automatically a broadcast channel. Observe yield results when loss matters and provide explicit early-stop behavior rather than assuming a loop break cancels every retained producer.
followUps: How would bufferingOldest(1) handle the same progress burst?
What other limit is needed if one value contains a very large payload?
pitfalls: Calling a buffer limit producer backpressure.
Dropping required ordered text fragments with newest-only buffering.

questions.prompt: What behavior changes in these two reactive/async bridges? Preserve the intended errors, start time, values, and producer lifetime.
questions.scenario: One publisher adapter ends AsyncStream normally when the publisher fails. A reverse adapter starts a Task sending to PassthroughSubject before returning the publisher. Subscriber cancellation never reaches the task handle.
questions.androidBridge: Converting RxJava or Kotlin Flow sources can likewise change errors, replay, start timing, and disposal. Combine demand and subject semantics differ from Flow collection, and Swift async iteration does not automatically preserve either library's failure or cancellation contract.
rubric: Identifies failure becoming normal completion as a visible change.
Explains how starting before subscription can lose early values.
Connects consumer termination to cleanup of bridge-owned producers.
Tests timing, errors, buffering, and cancellation as well as successful values.
questions.answerHTML:
Ending normally on failure erases the error. A best-effort notification source may allow that, but a data reader expecting failure loses its recovery signal. Use a throwing sequence when errors are part of the promise, or document the deliberate change. Test failure separately from normal completion. A bridge is equivalent only when callers observe the intended behavior, not merely a similar-looking return type.

The reverse adapter starts work before subscription, so a nonreplaying subject can miss early values. It also lacks a defined stop path if subscriber cancellation never reaches the producing task. Choose subscription-driven start or deliberate replay according to the source, and assign ownership of the producer handle. For the async side, connect termination to cleanup and provide an explicit stop when an early consumer exit otherwise retains the source.
